content:
Episode 11 — Kick-Start Your Writing Instruction (Overview)

The first 10 episodes have focused on planning lessons, delivering instruction, guiding practice, organizing units, and assessing progress. Here, in Episode 11 the focus shifts — BEFORE we can teach WRITING, we have to prepare students to be WRITERS.

And while it might seem like this should have been the topic of Episode 1 — it actually fits best here, at the end of the series. Now that you know the role of direct instruction and how it feeds what should be INDEPENDENT writing time, it's easier to appreciate the importance of creating the conditions where that can actually happen.

This episode is all about the KICK-START — the first 2 or 3 weeks BEFORE introducing the 3 modes, BEFORE diving into units, and BEFORE teaching standards-based skills.

While there are numerous procedures and routines that go into establishing an efficient and effective writing environment, I want to identify 6 that are essential for a strong start. Without deliberately addressing these, teaching writing will likely be a yearlong struggle for YOU and YOUR students.

Episode 11 — #1 Build Stamina: Why Stamina Matters

So much of building strong, independent writers is rooted in stamina. In fact, learning anything new is hard. That's not a flaw in the learner — that's the very nature of learning, in acquiring the ability to DO something you couldn't do before.

Trying anything for the first time is uncomfortable. It's usually slow-going. And it's often frustrating. In these situations, if the learner ALSO lacks habits & strategies to persevere, he tends to put forth little effort and/or generates a mediocre attempt. THIS is why developing students' writer stamina is so essential. Because during writing time practice students WILL get stuck. They WILL need help. They WILL get frustrated. And without strong writer habits & strategies to persevere, they WILL give up.

While it may appear that "kids today" may not want to write or don't want to work that hard, we have to assess if we've taught them HOW to persevere as writers. Explaining that students need to HAVE stamina doesn't mean they all of a sudden possess it. We have to provide opportunities for them to experience productive struggles in small doses COMBINED with strategies to overcome them.

section_name: #1 Build Stamina — Daily Goal, Visual Timer, Incremental Increase
content:
Episode 11 — #1 Build Stamina: Daily Minute Goals, Visual Timer, Incremental Increase

Here are 3 procedures that may be helpful in developing your students' writer stamina.

Identify the daily goal. Students have to know the target to shoot at it, so how many minutes are you expecting them to be able to write AFTER the mini-lesson. Here are some universal expectations.

After introducing the stamina GOAL, adjust TODAY'S TIME to honor their current LACK of writer muscle. Explain that each day, you will incrementally increase the minutes for Writing Time, as you are trying to stretch and GROW their muscles to be able to write or draw longer.

When announcing today's stamina goal, reveal a visual timer. Point out that it doesn't count DOWN. It won't ring or ding at Zero. It counts UP the seconds and minutes to see how long students can go — to measure how long they can stay focused on their topics and persevering as WRITERS.

On a related note, STAMINA is DEPENDENT on students writing regularly. While you may not be able to integrate writing instruction and practice EVERY day, students can't go too many days without it. Stamina is like a muscle — it only grows with consistent exercise. The more often students write, the stronger their stamina becomes. But when writing happens sporadically, growth and development start to fade.
skill_title: Daily Goal, Visual Timer, Incremental Increase

section_name: #1 Build Stamina — Break Down the Writing Time & Chart Growth
content:
Episode 11 — #1 Build Stamina: Break Down the Writing Time & Chart Growth

A second strategy to support stamina growth is to break down the writing time. Even a short chunk of forced writing — like five minutes — can feel overwhelming. When students are out of writing shape, any amount of time can feel impossible. So, instead of simply saying, "Write for five minutes," give them a plan for how to USE those minutes.

For example, older writers might:
- Spend the first 30 seconds INDEPENDENTLY thinking about the topic. Maybe even with their eyes closed to block out distractions.
- Then, spend the next 90 seconds INDEPENDENTLY listing the key points or details.
- Before using the remaining 3 minutes to INDEPENDENTLY write or type them out.

This approach works across the grade levels. Early writers might think quietly, then turn and tell a friend their idea, before drawing it out on their OWN papers.

By suggesting to students how they might break down even a short Writing Time can make a stamina goal more achievable.

Additionally, find a way to chart their GROWING stamina. Whether it's a class chart, an individual graph, or a simple sticky-note scoreboard, give students a way to SEE their stamina building. Challenge them to beat their previous time — even if it's just by a few seconds.
skill_title: Break Down the Writing Time & Chart Growth

content:
Episode 11 — #2 Troubleshoot Spelling & Transcription

In addition to stretching their stamina, students ALSO need practical strategies to lean on when they hit obstacles during independent writing time. Three common struggle points that can impede students from writing are: getting tripped up by transcription and spelling, needing help when they have a question, and being "done" and not knowing what to do next. We must anticipate each of these writer needs and develop students' capacity to work through them.

If students know WHAT they want to say but struggle to get it written or typed before fatigue sets in, then this often points to a weakness in transcription skills. Depending on the grade level, this might include:
- Struggling to form letters quickly and easily
- Feeling discomfort or pain when gripping a pencil
- Possessing limited or inefficient keyboarding skills
- Struggling to sound out word spellings
- Hesitating to take spelling risks

The research reveals that when students struggle with any of these foundational transcription skills, their cognitive resources are diverted from higher-level writing tasks, making composition more difficult.

When a student doesn't know how to spell a word, he can't finish his sentence or write the next one. This is a trigger that shuts down some writers. Now a teacher's first instinct may be to PROVIDE a student with the correct spelling as a quick fix to get him back to writing. BUT, over time, this creates a dependency on the teacher — a bad habit that is hard to break. Similarly, we don't want to direct older students to "look up" words in a dictionary. While appropriate for the editing stage, stopping to search for a word DURING first-draft writing disrupts a student's flow of ideas — breaking his writing momentum.

A stronger approach is to provide students with a set of FIRST DRAFT strategies to TEMPORARILY resolve their spelling challenge, allowing them to capture their ideas BEFORE pausing to edit the spelling. One way to do this is by creating a "stuck-spelling strategies" list — a grade-level set of options for students to employ independently when they aren't sure how to spell a word in the FIRST DRAFT.

This posted list would include stretching the word and listening for sounds, along with several other options. Identify those that are appropriate for your students' current level of spelling knowledge. For example, older students this might include breaking the word into syllables or listening for roots like prefixes and suffixes. Additionally, this same strategy satisfies the spelling perfectionists. Knowing that YOU, the teacher, don't spell words forces them to seek out another strategy. Emphasize that they WILL look up the word or spell check it later, when editing, but NOT when drafting. That's NOT how writers work.

By developing students' independent first-draft spelling habits, we support their ability to persevere when writing gets hard, further increasing their stamina.

section_name: #3 Provide Help — Managing Frustration & the Help Tent
content:
Episode 11 — #3 Provide Help: Managing Frustration & the Help Tent

While spelling and transcription are very SPECIFIC obstacles, another struggle to anticipate is the more GENERAL need for help. Questions are a natural part of learning. But getting stuck isn't just a mental problem — it's an emotional one, too. Frustration builds fast. And when students feel stuck, it doesn't take long for some of them to melt down or shut down.

Writing isn't just a brain task — it's a heart task, too. Strong writers don't just learn skills, they learn how to manage their mindset while writing. We want to teach students that frustration isn't failure; it's part of the process.

List activities they're good at — video games, braiding hair, TikTok dances, drawing, playing sports. Then, remind them that they didn't wake up good at those things. They practiced. They messed up. They kept going. It wasn't perfect the first time or the second or even the third. But now, after time and lots of practice, those are skills they feel confident about.

Learning how to write works the same way. Some days may start fine — where they are going through the task, they're on a roll and feeling confident. But then what WAS simple gets hard and STOPS them. They may think, "This is too hard, I CAN'T do this" or "Forget it, I'm done."

These feelings are normal. Learning new things IS hard, but we want them to ask for help BEFORE they hit their breaking point. That's why we need to teach both a procedure for seeking help AND the habits for managing their frustration. This yellow zone is critical. It's the key to keeping students moving forward.

One such strategy is the HELP tent. When a writer is stuck or has a question, he quietly pops it up on his desk, silently signaling to the teacher: "I need help." NOW, the students can ask for help, but the reality is there's one of you and 20+ of them. Consequently, Help tents have two sides. The back side lists several strategies students can try while waiting. Being stuck doesn't mean stopping.

Writers keep going with what they CAN do. They might:
- Check an anchor chart or resource
- Ask a friend
- Skip that part for now and work on another part
- Reread what they've written and add more

The Help Tent validates that it's normal to get stuck and have questions — but that doesn't mean you stop trying. None of the options suggest "sit and do nothing" or "make a line at the teacher's desk."

Provide writers with strategies to try until help arrives. We want them to push through, to try different solutions, and to keep working. Our goal is that they begin to develop habits for problem-solving and persevering, and by the time we get to them, they may have even answered their own question.

If we don't teach students what to do when they hit a writing roadblock, they'll often default to weak habits like waiting, crying, erupting, or interrupting. The critical yellow zone is where we can build their perseverance and grit.

Episode 11 — #4 Redefine Done: The Done List

This same persistence is needed when students think they've finished writing. We need to challenge this idea of being "done." When students declare they're "done," it often means they've completed the task but don't know what to do next or what else to add.

"Done" writers are task-oriented; they are git-r-done kids, so simply encouraging them to "reread and make it better" doesn't provide enough motivation or direction for these students. To help them keep working on the same piece, we need to identify specific actions that they can take to further develop their writing.

This is where the "Done" list comes in — post a visible and tangible list of simple revision tasks students already know but need reminders to apply. These tasks help students re-enter their drafts and keep working. The "Done" list might include tasks such as:
- Strikethrough two weak words with a purple pen and replace them with stronger ones.
- Insert 2 sensory details with a red pen.
- Highlight all transition words and revise for repetition.
- Try out 3 new titles on a sticky note and pick your favorite.

These tasks are ideal for "fast" writers, you know, the git-r-done kids. Because they are specific, measurable, and achievable. We want students to recognize that "done" is simply a pause point, not the final step of the process.

For older students, the "Done" list should focus more on revision strategies — emphasizing content and organization over grammar and mechanics. However, for younger writers or multilingual learners, the list SHOULD include some simpler editing tasks. We want to make sure it's readable before pushing them to write more. And depending on their WIDA level, the Done list for early writers might include some pictorial tasks, too. For example:
- Add three small details to the person or topic you drew.
- S-l-o-w-l-y read aloud each word label, listening for additional sounds/letters you could write.
- Check for spaces between words.
- Add a color word as an adjective before 3 different nouns.

The Done list sends a clear message to "fast" writers — or those who finish early — that there's still more work to do. Encourage them to keep selecting tasks from the list until writing time ends. Colored pens, sticky notes, and highlighters can boost student engagement when revising on paper. Plus, the more tasks listed, the more choice students have — allowing them to personalize their revision process.

Ultimately, the Done list helps students realize there is always more they can do to add and to improve their writing. Over time, they begin to view revision as a natural part of writing — keeping them engaged longer and developing their skills further.

section_name: #5 Meet to Teach — Introducing the Mini-Lesson Routine
content:
Episode 11 — #5 Meet to Teach: Introducing the Mini-Lesson Routine

Each of the procedures for troubleshooting spelling, providing help, and redefining done equips students with problem-solving strategies that real writers use. Instead of feeling stuck, students now know how to tackle and overcome these obstacles, causing their confidence to grow, their stamina to build, and slowly but surely, they stop groaning when it's time to write.

In addition to building writer habits with those 4 lessons, the opening weeks of writing instruction also need to establish the routine that EVERY writing time is preceded with a short class meeting.

You'll want to describe how a lesson works. Remember — your students had a different teacher last year, and she may have executed writing lessons very differently. While you may have a solid handle on what a Mini-Lesson IS, your students likely don't. That's why Lesson 5 is essential.

This procedural lesson includes explaining that every writing block begins the same way: with YOU teaching THEM something about being a WRITER or improving their WRITING. Roll out what a 15-min mini-lesson looks, sounds, and feels like. Orient students to its predictable rhythm and clear expectations.

This includes explaining that a mini-lesson is led by you — the teacher. It's not a class discussion. It's a short, focused time for YOU to name, explain, and model a skill that will guide today's writing time.
- This is where you clearly articulate roles. YOUR ROLE is to SHOW them how to do something. THEIR role is to watch and listen.
- Tell them that you won't be calling on volunteers to help. Make it clear that you'll do the first example ALL by yourself.
- Then, the second example, you will prompt them to turn, talk, and orally TRY the skill with a peer.
- Introduce the code phrases — T&T and B2M. Let students know that this back-and-forth gives them a little experience with the skill before they are asked to transfer into their own writing.

The Mini-Lesson and Writing Time are the heartbeat of every writing block. First, I teach. Then, you try. That's the daily rhythm.

section_name: #6 Time to Write — Writing Time Transition & Closing
content:
Episode 11 — #6 Time to Write: Writing Time Transition & Closing

After the mini-lesson wraps, there's a clear transition from students listening and watching to students trying and writing. That shift is often signaled with a code phrase like: "Now it's your turn" or "Let's go be writers."

Writing Time is where students take on the "you do" task — applying the skill or strategy that was just modeled in the mini-lesson. It's their time to experiment, attempt, and practice as writers. Once the writing task is announced, students begin.
- And if they have a question, they pop up the Help Tent — but keep working while they wait.
- Or if they get stuck on spelling, they glance up at the Stuck Spelling list — knowing the teacher doesn't spell words.
- And if they finish early, they turn to the Done List — re-entering the writing, pushing it further.

THIS is where the procedures & problem-solving strategies you've introduced will pay off. A productive writing time requires procedures AND sustained effort from students. Stamina fuels practice, and practice builds skill.

As I wrap up this video, let me highlight the key takeaway: While there are MANY different routines and expectations that teachers roll out at the beginning of the year, we must include a set of procedures that support students' physical, mental, and emotional struggles during writing time. Consequently, I encourage you to think ahead to the start of next school year by reflecting on your current routines, evaluating what worked and what didn't, and even gathering feedback from students about their writer needs. With a focus on growing students' stamina and building strong habits, we take the next step toward building better writers.
